title: George Lewis's funeral: playing in the band and the church service
summary: Green describes preparing to play and the church service as ritual.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: I think it's a great question. Let's, let's, let's, we can perhaps change the subject a little. Um, George's funeral was on Friday and you were not only there but playing in one of the bands. And perhaps you can, I mean this is, we're fairly close to this right now but you know in years of time people will want to know about the funeral I think. Perhaps you can say something about it and, uh, as you brought back in. The general, just describe what happened.

Well, like all New Orleans funerals, playing, I'm playing my bad borrowed cornet. It's not, it wasn't a bad cornet, I play it badly. Uh, meeting on the street corner. There's somewhat of a feeling that it's frivolous, I think. Uh, I'm not, in my tradition I'm not used to funerals being that much of a party. What impressed me so much, starting off at the hall with the Japanese and the Swedes and Frank DeMond and Charlie DeVore who'd come in from Minneapolis, starting this band was, how wonderful this is. What we are concerned is not a funeral but are our instruments okay? The drummer didn't have a strap for his drum, he had to fashion it out of a rope. Concerned with, was the head of the drum tight? Whose cornet? Were there enough, was there, did the mouthpiece fit? We were concerned with the trade of the man who was being buried and in that sense it was a continuation. And therefore, at that moment I realized my whole concept of funeral has to change. That this was acting out something. It was almost, I felt a ritualistic dance. This getting ready, it was George Lewis's last gig. This is what it felt like. And we were gonna play at George's last gig. And it was much more like a jazz job than a funeral. Although there was no pay involved.
Yes. Did you, um, were you in the church?

I was in the church, uh, of course as you know there was a gentle rain, it was misty, and, and a very Japanese weather as a matter of fact. Everything was very soft, very gray. Uh, went into the church, surprisingly found a seat, and stayed for the funeral. And then outside into the rain again.
What did you, what, uh, can you describe the service?

Uh, again I got the feeling of a ritualistic dance or chant rather than a service. I listened to the minister, uh, he started reading text, it didn't really make much sense, it didn't have much continuity, just as pure English. It didn't have much to do with George Lewis. And then his reading gradually began to take on rhythmic overtones, and it became a chant. And you felt that if it were only kept up a little longer, the whole audience would let go. It was, it was a catharsis. It was an emotional experience. What about the singing? The singing I wasn't overly impressed by. Wasn't overly impressed by. There were six other preachers there, and the dean of Winchester Cathedral would come to the church. And then from the center, sure. But I did think of, in the church of Papa John, once in Japan, I said to Papa John Joseph, who at 89 ought to know, I said, Papa John, you ought to know, where did jazz come from?
